title: Research note: Examining potential bias in large-scale censored data
screen_reason: Reports quantitative shares of Facebook-referred clicks that went to fake-news domains, in a representative uncensored panel (2.5%) and in the censored Facebook URLs dataset (10%), plus an appendix analysis giving fact-checked-false URLs as a share of all unique URLs and of all public shares on Facebook. These are EXPOSURE (share of consumed clicks), CONTENT (share of URLs that exist) and SHARING (share of public shares) estimates with explicit denominators.

estimates.platform: Facebook (clicks from Facebook newsfeed, observed in Nielsen desktop panel)
estimates.measure_type: % of clicks from the Facebook newsfeed that went to fake-news domains (uncensored, representative panel)
estimates.value_raw: 2.5% of clicks were to fake news (24% not-fake news, 74% not-news); Table 1 Column A
estimates.denominator: clicks from the Facebook newsfeed by Nielsen desktop panelists in December 2018, measured on a random sample of 1,000 URLs visited by panelists with the 'fbclid' parameter
estimates.definition: the clicked URL's domain appeared on a list of 624 fake-news websites
estimates.misinfo_def: "The list of fake news sites was composed of the 624 websites previously identified by researchers, professional fact checkers, and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality, or hyperpartisan news."
estimates.n: 1,000 URLs (random sample of Nielsen URLs clicked from Facebook newsfeed, December 2018)
estimates.source_quote: Following this procedure, we found that 2.5% of clicks were to fake news, 24% of clicks were to not-fake news, and 74% of clicks were to not-news sites (shown in Column A in Table 1).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain lists reused from Allen et al. (2020): 9,000+ 'not-fake' hard-news sites and 624 fake-news sites previously identified by researchers, professional fact checkers and journalists; all other domains coded not-news. No inter-coder reliability reported (list-based classification).
estimates.moderator_quote: We then took a random sample of 1,000 URLs from Nielsen visited by our panelists, clicked from Facebook newsfeed, during the same month. Unlike the Facebook dataset, we observed all the URLs that people visit rather than a censored version of URLs with greater than 100 public shares.
estimates.notes: This is the paper's uncensored, nationally representative benchmark estimate and the one an evidence synthesis should use. Denominator is ALL Facebook-referred clicks (retail, social media, etc. included), not just news, so denom_scope = all_media. Robustness re-run with de-duplicated clicks and a stricter Facebook-referral definition gave 2.6% (Appendix 3C) — same estimate, not a separate row.

estimates.measure_type: % of clicks on Facebook that went to fake-news domains, in the censored Facebook URLs dataset (URLs with >=100 public shares only)
estimates.value_raw: 10% of clicks went to fake news (38% not-fake news, 52% not-news); Table 1 Column B
estimates.denominator: all clicks by U.S. users on URLs contained in the Facebook URLs dataset in December 2018 (dataset restricted to URLs shared publicly by 100+ users); total clicks not reported
estimates.definition: the clicked URL's domain appeared on a list of 624 fake-news websites
estimates.misinfo_def: "The list of fake news sites was composed of the 624 websites previously identified by researchers, professional fact checkers, and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality, or hyperpartisan news."
estimates.n: not reported (aggregate U.S. clicks in the Facebook URLs dataset, December 2018)
estimates.source_quote: In that month of the Facebook dataset, we found that 10% of clicks went to fake news, 38% of clicks went to not-fake news, and 52% of clicks went to not-news sites (shown in Column B in Table 1).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same domain lists as the Nielsen row (624 fake-news sites, 9,000+ hard-news sites); no reliability statistics.
estimates.moderator_quote: Additionally, Facebook restricted URLs in this dataset to those that have been shared publicly by 100 different users (plus Laplace[5] noise to minimize information leakage).
estimates.notes: Same country x platform x measure cell as the 2.5% row; the difference is the data source's censoring, so definition_variant = true and denom_selection = curated (the denominator is truncated to URLs above a 100-public-share threshold). The authors present this as an OVERESTIMATE (~4x). The paper also reports a 1/2017-12/2018 average from the same censored dataset ('an average of 12% of clicks per month went to fake news content'); per the time-series rule that series is collapsed to this December 2018 point, chosen because it is the month matched to Nielsen and the Table 1 headline.

estimates.platform: Facebook (Nielsen panel clicks, restricted to URLs present in the Facebook URLs dataset)
estimates.measure_type: % of Facebook-referred clicks that went to fake news, after dropping panel URLs absent from the censored Facebook URLs dataset
estimates.value_raw: 7% were fake news (39% not-fake news, 55% not-news); Table 1 Column C
estimates.denominator: the subset of the 1,000 sampled Nielsen Facebook-referred URLs that could be matched in the Facebook URLs dataset (i.e. that met the 100-public-share threshold), December 2018
estimates.definition: the clicked URL's domain appeared on a list of 624 fake-news websites
estimates.misinfo_def: "The list of fake news sites was composed of the 624 websites previously identified by researchers, professional fact checkers, and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality, or hyperpartisan news."
estimates.n: matched subset of 1,000 sampled URLs (84% of fake-news URLs, 50% of not-fake-news URLs and 23% of not-news URLs matched; matched total not stated)
estimates.source_quote: dropping the Nielsen URLs without Facebook matches—we found that 7% were fake news
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same domain lists (624 fake-news sites); matching to the Facebook URLs dataset used as a proxy for having met the 100-public-share threshold.
estimates.moderator_quote: We found that 84% of fake news URLs in our Nielsen sample were also present in the Facebook dataset, but only 50% of not-fake news URLs and 23% of not-news URLs were.
estimates.notes: A deliberate simulation of censoring inside the representative panel, not an independent prevalence estimate; kept because it is a distinct definition variant (same panel, censored denominator) and is Table 1 Column C. An adjudicator may prefer to drop it as a methodological demonstration. Exact matched denominator not reported.

estimates.platform: Facebook (Nielsen panel clicks, restricted to URLs with >100 CrowdTangle public shares)
estimates.measure_type: % of Facebook-referred clicks that went to fake news, among URLs above a 100 CrowdTangle public-share threshold
estimates.value_raw: 7% of clicks were to fake news sites (42% not-fake news, 51% non-news); Table 1 Column D
estimates.denominator: the subset of sampled Nielsen Facebook-referred URLs (December 2018) with more than 100 CrowdTangle public shares since January 2017
estimates.definition: the clicked URL's domain appeared on a list of 624 fake-news websites
estimates.misinfo_def: "The list of fake news sites was composed of the 624 websites previously identified by researchers, professional fact checkers, and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality, or hyperpartisan news."
estimates.n: subset of the 1,000 sampled Nielsen URLs above 100 CrowdTangle public shares (size not reported)
estimates.source_quote: Above the 100 CrowdTangle share threshold, 7% of clicks were to fake news sites, 42% of clicks were to not-fake news sites, and 51% of clicks were to non-news sites.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 624-site fake-news domain list; CrowdTangle API used to count public shares by public pages, groups and public profiles (a lower bound on Facebook public shares).
estimates.moderator_quote: Unfortunately, CrowdTangle has a more restrictive definition for public shares than Facebook does. CrowdTangle share counts are limited to only those articles shared by public pages, groups, or users with “public” profiles, who usually are public figures like politicians or celebrities.
estimates.notes: Second censoring simulation (CrowdTangle threshold rather than Facebook-dataset matching). The threshold sweep also reports the same measure to one decimal, 'the percent of all URL content that was fake news also increased from 5.1% to 7.4%' as the threshold went from 1 to 100 CrowdTangle shares; 7.4% is this row's 7% and is not entered twice.

estimates.platform: Facebook (Nielsen panel clicks with >=1 CrowdTangle public share)
estimates.measure_type: % of Facebook-referred NEWS clicks that went to fake news (news denominator, minimal censoring: >=1 CrowdTangle public share)
estimates.value_raw: "the percent of news that was fake went from 11.5% to 15%" (11.5% at a 1 CrowdTangle-share threshold; 15% at 100)
estimates.denominator: clicks to news domains (fake + not-fake news) among sampled Nielsen Facebook-referred URLs with at least 1 CrowdTangle public share, December 2018
estimates.definition: the clicked news URL's domain appeared on the 624-site fake-news list
estimates.misinfo_def: "The list of fake news sites was composed of the 624 websites previously identified by researchers, professional fact checkers, and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality, or hyperpartisan news."
estimates.n: news clicks within the 1,000-URL Nielsen sample above 1 CrowdTangle share (size not reported)
estimates.source_quote: Similarly, the percent of news that was fake went from 11.5% to 15%, a 36% increase.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 624-site fake-news domain list against a 9,000+-site hard-news list; CrowdTangle public-share counts define the threshold.
estimates.moderator_quote: While most of the change occurred from 0 to 1 share, the percent of all URL content that was fake news also increased from 5.1% to 7.4% –a 45% increase–as the threshold changed from 1 CrowdTangle share to 100.
estimates.notes: Kept because it is the only NEWS-denominator (news_diet) figure stated verbatim: the fake share of news consumption. Both endpoints of the threshold sweep are verbatim; the least-censored one (>=1 CrowdTangle share, 11.5%) is entered and the 100-share endpoint (15%) recorded in value_raw rather than as a second row. Note the fully uncensored equivalent is NOT computed here: 2.5/(2.5+24) would be a cross-category ratio, which R8 forbids.

estimates.platform: Facebook (all URLs shared on the platform; internal Facebook analysis)
estimates.measure_type: % of all unique URLs shared on Facebook that were rated false by third-party fact-checkers (no share threshold)
estimates.value_raw: 37,860 false URLs of 16.2 bil. unique URLs = 0.00023% (Table A1, 'No Threshold'); 8,660 of 38.2 mil. = 0.022% above the 100-share threshold
estimates.denominator: 16.2 billion unique URLs shared on Facebook between 1/1/2017 and 12/31/2018 with no public-share threshold applied
estimates.definition: the individual URL had been labelled false by Facebook's third-party fact-checker program (URL-level, not publisher-level)
estimates.misinfo_def: "researchers at Facebook examined the URLs labeled as false by their third-party fact-checker program from 1/1/2017-12/31/2018"
estimates.source_quote: The Facebook team found that the number of unique false news URLs as a proportion of all unique URLs in the dataset increased by two orders of magnitude when a 100 public share threshold was implemented, going from 0.00023% with no threshold to 0.022% with one (a two-magnitude increase).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Facebook's third-party fact-checking program, applied at the individual-URL level; no reliability statistics reported. Analysis run internally by Facebook researchers in response to the authors' findings.
estimates.moderator_quote: Additionally, they defined URLs as false on the URL level rather than domain level, since they as a rule did not want to perform analysis on the de-anonymized data based on an external research team’s domain list
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL for the adjudicator: this analysis was performed by Facebook researchers at the authors' request and is reported for the first time in this paper's Appendix 1 (see Competing interests: 'Facebook researchers performed the analysis in Appendix Section 1'), so it is treated as original to this paper rather than a figure cited from elsewhere. Also note the scope is platform-wide (not U.S.-only) and unstated by country, hence Global; the denominator is every URL shared on Facebook, including non-news, which is why the value is so small; and only individually fact-checked URLs count as false, the strictest possible numerator.

estimates.platform: Facebook (all public URL shares; internal Facebook analysis)
estimates.measure_type: % of all public URL shares on Facebook that were shares of URLs rated false by third-party fact-checkers (no share threshold)
estimates.value_raw: 30.5 mil. false-URL public shares of 33.7 bil. public shares = 0.091% (Table A1, 'No Threshold'); 30.3 mil. of 16.3 bil. = 0.185% above the 100-share threshold
estimates.denominator: 33.7 billion public URL shares on Facebook between 1/1/2017 and 12/31/2018 with no public-share threshold applied
estimates.definition: the shared URL had been labelled false by Facebook's third-party fact-checker program
estimates.misinfo_def: "researchers at Facebook examined the URLs labeled as false by their third-party fact-checker program from 1/1/2017-12/31/2018"
estimates.source_quote: Additionally, when the researchers focused on the total public URL shares (a closer analog to the click analysis that we did previously, but clicks are more common than shares) rather than the number of unique URLs, they found that the proportion of false news URLs shares doubled with the 100-share threshold, going from 0.091% with no threshold to 0.185% with the 100-share threshold.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Facebook's third-party fact-checking program at the individual-URL level; internal Facebook analysis; no reliability statistics.
estimates.moderator_quote: There are 30,500,000 public shares of the 37,860 unique false URLs, yet 30,300,000 of those public shares come from the 8,660 unique false URLs that have over 100-shares.
estimates.notes: Share-weighted counterpart of the previous row: the denominator is public share EVENTS, so the construct is SHARING (content_share), not CONTENT. Same judgement call about the Facebook-internal provenance. unit coded url because each event is a public share of a URL. Whole-platform, no country breakdown.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 'From 1/2017-12/2018, an average of 12% of clicks per month went to fake news content, 32% went to not-fake news content, and 56% went to other, not-news content' - the same censored-dataset measure over a longer window; collapsed into the December 2018 row (10%) per the time-series rule. (2) Robustness re-run with de-duplicated clicks and a stricter Facebook-referral definition: '2.6% of clicks going to fake news' - the same estimate as the 2.5% row, not a distinct row. (3) Match rates ('84% of fake news URLs in our Nielsen sample were also present in the Facebook dataset, but only 50% of not-fake news URLs and 23% of not-news URLs were') are dataset-inclusion probabilities, not misinformation prevalence, so no row. (4) '5.1% to 7.4%' fake-news share of clicks across the CrowdTangle 1-to-100 sweep duplicates the 7% Table 1 Column D row. (5) The 15% endpoint of 'the percent of news that was fake' sweep is recorded in value_raw rather than as a second row. (6) Appendix 2 Table A2 gives news (14.9% Nielsen vs 33.3% Facebook) and other category shares of clicks but collapses fake and not-fake news together, so it carries no misinformation estimate. (7) 'approximately 30% of not-fake news URLs' had 0 CrowdTangle shares - not a misinformation share. (8) Figure 1 and Figure 2 are images in the source and could not be read; all values entered come from the running text or Tables 1/A1.

rob.design: Comparison of two data sources for U.S. Facebook clicks, December 2018 (and 1/2017-12/2018 for the censored series): (a) Facebook Social Science One URLs dataset - platform census restricted to URLs shared publicly by 100+ users, engagement counts perturbed with differentially private noise and de-duplicated to one action per user per URL; (b) Nielsen nationally representative desktop web panel, all URLs visited, Facebook referrals identified by the 'fbclid' parameter, from which a random sample of 1,000 URLs was drawn. Classification by pre-existing domain lists (9,000+ hard-news sites; 624 fake-news sites; all else not-news), so no human coding and no inter-coder reliability statistics are reported; no response rate reported for the Nielsen panel; desktop-only panel vs mobile-inclusive platform data is an acknowledged asymmetry. Robustness checks: de-duplication, stricter referral definition, CrowdTangle share counts, and an internal Facebook URL-level fact-check analysis (Appendix 1).
rob.item6_quote: The list of fake news sites was composed of the 624 websites previously identified by researchers, professional fact checkers, and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality, or hyperpartisan news.
rob.item10_quote: Following this procedure, we found that 2.5% of clicks were to fake news, 24% of clicks were to not-fake news, and 74% of clicks were to not-news sites (shown in Column A in Table 1).
